title: Russia Turns Ukraine's Gas Stations Into Deadly Targets in Escalating Drone War
excerpt: Over 200 fuel stations have been hit in two months as Moscow retaliates for Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries that have triggered fuel shortages from Crimea to Siberia.
body:
• Russia has struck over 200 Ukrainian gas stations in June and July — roughly three per day — concentrating attacks on frontline regions within easy drone range.
  • Zaporizhzhia alone suffered 54 strikes on fuel stations in a 24-day period through July 27, killing four and injuring 29 people.
  • The campaign is widely seen as retaliation for Ukraine's long-range drone strikes on Russian refineries, which have triggered nationwide fuel shortages with queues of up to 18 hours in some regions.
  • Ukrainian officials say the attacks are "deliberate terrorism" targeting civilian infrastructure with no military significance.

Policeman Mykhailo Tsypliakov was already running toward the burning gas station when he heard the buzz of a second drone descending. He hit the ground. "I saw a flash, then got up right away," he told CNN. "I saw that my arm, legs and torso were injured."

Tsypliakov is one of dozens of victims of Russia's latest campaign against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure. Over the past two months, Russian forces have systematically targeted fuel stations across the country, hitting more than 200 since June — an average of about three per day, according to Ukrainian officials.

A New Front in the Drone War

The attacks have concentrated on gas stations near the front lines, within the operational range of Russia's first-person-view (FPV) attack drones. But airstrikes, longer-distance drones, and cruise missiles have extended the toll to stations near Kyiv and other cities far from the contact line.

https://x.com/ZelenskyyUa/status/2084608193645146204

Regina Kharchenko, acting mayor of Zaporizhzhia, said her city endured 54 strikes targeting gas stations in a 24-day period through July 27. The attacks killed four people and injured 29. "This is deliberate terrorism targeting civilian infrastructure and civilians," she said. "Russia is deliberately targeting facilities that have no military significance but are essential to the daily functioning of a big city."

Kramatorsk, increasingly close to Russia's inch-by-inch advances through the Donbas, and Kharkiv, near the Russian border, have also been heavily hit. A CNN analysis located and confirmed at least 30 videos of strikes on gas stations across the country in June and July alone.

More Than Just Fuel Pumps

In a country where commercial air travel is impossible and vast distances are connected by road and rail, gas stations have taken on an outsized role as community hubs. Yaroslav Starovoitenko, president of the Ukrainian Oil and Gas Association, explained the stations' significance during the war.

"Gas stations became these key points of refuge as people fled the war. They had generators, always on. These were places where people could drink hot tea, fill up their cars, warm up, and even prepare milk for their babies."

— Yaroslav Starovoitenko, President, Ukrainian Oil and Gas Association

Moscow has not been shy about showcasing the attacks. Russia's elite drone unit, Rubicon, posted a video this month highlighting nine strikes on gas stations in the Kharkiv and Sumy regions.

The Tit-for-Tat Logic

Ukrainian officials believe the campaign is a direct response to Kyiv's intensifying long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries and energy infrastructure. Those attacks have triggered fuel shortages across much of Russia, with restrictions imposed from Crimea to Siberia.

In Moscow, extraordinary scenes have emerged of cars and trucks lining up outside gas stations, with some drivers waiting for hours. Russian media reported queues of up to 18 hours in some regions. Tatneft, Russia's fifth-biggest oil company, became the first retailer to impose nationwide fuel purchase caps, limiting sales to 20 litres of petrol per car at some stations.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's defence minister, acknowledged the retaliatory logic. "Russia aimed to destroy all our frontline filling stations" in response to Ukrainian attacks on Russia's logistics, he said on Telegram, adding that "civilian filling stations have absolutely no impact on military fuel supplies. The aim of the attacks is to terrorise the civilian population."

One Ukrainian official put it more bluntly: "People used to joke that Russia is a 'gas station country,' but in reality, this 'gas station country' has run out of gas. We see huge lines at gas stations. The attacks are aimed at showing their own people, 'Look, it's even worse in Ukraine.'"

Defiance Amid the Danger

Despite the attacks, Ukrainians near Kyiv showed little sign of panic. At a gas station outside the capital, Serhiy, a wounded veteran, joked about the threat. "If a strike comes here, what's the difference? It didn't kill me on the front line, so it won't kill me here."

Vladyslav, a delivery driver, was more pragmatic: "No one knows where the attack will strike. But I'm working. I can't just not go."

Escalation Without End

The widening assault on civilian targets comes as Western officials warn of possible further escalation from Russian President Vladimir Putin. June was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since 2022, according to the United Nations. Russia launched record numbers of ballistic missiles in recent weeks, including a devastating overnight strike on Kyiv on August 2 that killed at least nine people and wounded more than 30.

Four years into the full-scale invasion, the war's logic has settled into a grim pattern: each side targets the other's civilian infrastructure to raise the domestic cost of continuing the fight. For now, neither side shows any sign of blinking.
